llm_response.content:
Below is a complete empirical plan tailored to the Danish administrative data and the question of how the arrival of children affects gender inequality in the labor market.

1. Identification Strategy
- Method: Event-study difference-in-differences (triple difference) centered on the birth of the first child, comparing outcomes of mothers versus fathers within the same couple over time.
- Rationale:
  - The first birth provides a sharp and well-timed event.
  - Comparing mothers to fathers within the same couple tightly controls for household-level shocks, selection into parenthood, and many time-varying confounders that affect both parents.
  - An event-study with leads and lags allows visualization and testing of pre-trends and estimation of dynamic (short- and long-run) effects.
  - Denmark’s high-quality registers precisely measure event timing and outcomes, strengthening the design.

2. Treatment and Control
- Treatment variable: Being the mother (female parent) in years at and after the birth of the couple’s first child. Operationalized via interactions Female × 1{event time k}, k ≥ 0.
- Control group:
  - Primary: The father in the same couple (male parent), at the same event times. This yields a mother-minus-father causal contrast in response to childbirth.
  - Pre-period for both parents serves as baseline (event time k < 0).
- Treatment timing / event date: Year of the couple’s first live birth. Event time τct = year t − first_birth_yearc. We typically use a symmetric window, e.g., τ ∈ [−5, +15]. We will exclude τ = −1 as the reference (or, for robustness, τ ∈ {−2, −1} as pre-baseline to account for pregnancy anticipatory effects).
- RDD: Not used.

3. Key Identifying Assumptions
- Parallel trends within couples (counterfactual): In the absence of a birth, mothers and fathers in the same couple would have followed parallel trends in outcomes near the event. Plausibility: Strong in Denmark, since both partners are of similar age, share location and household shocks; we can assess with pre-trends (event-time leads).
- No other gender-differential shocks exactly coincident with birth, beyond the causal channels we wish to capture (parental leave, caregiving). Plausibility: Danish parental leave is part of the mechanism of interest. Policy changes over calendar time are addressed by calendar-year fixed effects and child-cohort-by-gender controls.
- Accurate timing and measurement: Registers accurately record biological parent links, birth dates, and earnings/employment. Plausibility: High in Denmark.
- Stable composition and minimal differential attrition: We can follow both parents over long horizons; if separation occurs, parent identities remain. Plausibility: Reasonable; we will check selection and use robustness (balanced windows, IPW).
- SUTVA/no spillovers across couples: One couple’s childbirth does not affect another couple’s outcomes in ways correlated with our design. Plausibility: High.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
- Anticipation and pregnancy effects (women adjust in τ = −1 and possibly −2):
  - Mitigation: Exclude τ = −1 from baseline; show event-study leads (τ ≤ −2) are flat; re-estimate with τ ∈ {−2, −1} as the omitted category; optionally drop the pregnancy year(s) when estimating long-run effects.
- Differential selection/attrition (e.g., separation, migration, missing earnings during leave):
  - Mitigation: Intent-to-treat by keeping biological parents irrespective of marital status; include all observed years even if parents separate; use inverse probability weights for remaining observed in long-run windows; show robustness on balanced panels; test sensitivity to excluding couples with separation within X years post-birth.
- Time-varying confounding by policy and macro shocks:
  - Mitigation: Include calendar-year fixed effects, parent age polynomials interacted with gender, and first-birth cohort (child birth year) by gender fixed effects; estimate effects within narrower child-cohort bins; show robustness splitting pre/post major policy reforms.

5. R Code Outline
Note: Replace file names/variable names with actual Danish register names. The outline assumes CSV inputs with minimal necessary fields.

Packages
- fixest for high-dimensional FE and event-study
- data.table for manipulation
- ggplot2 for plots

Code
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)

# 1) Load data (toy file names; adjust to your context)
ind <- fread("individuals.csv")        # id, sex (F/M), yob
earn <- fread("earnings.csv")          # id, year, earnings, employed (0/1), hours
births <- fread("birth_links.csv")     # child_id, mother_id, father_id, child_birth_year
# Optional: couple registry if needed to validate partners
# couples <- fread("couples.csv")     # couple start/end years, etc.

# 2) Construct first-birth at the couple level
# Keep first biological child per mother-father pair
births <- births[!is.na(mother_id) & !is.na(father_id)]
births[, couple_id := paste0(mother_id, "_", father_id)]
firstb <- births[, .(first_birth_year = min(child_birth_year)), by = couple_id]

# 3) Build parent-level panel around the first birth
# Prepare parent information
parents <- unique(births[, .(mother_id, father_id, couple_id)])
moms <- data.table(id = parents$mother_id, couple_id = parents$couple_id, female = 1L)
dads <- data.table(id = parents$father_id, couple_id = parents$couple_id, female = 0L)
par_long <- rbind(moms, dads, use.names = TRUE)

# Merge first-birth year onto parents
par_long <- merge(par_long, firstb, by = "couple_id", all.x = TRUE)

# Merge earnings
y <- merge(par_long, earn, by = "id", allow.cartesian = TRUE)
# Construct event time
y[, event_time := year - first_birth_year]

# Keep event window, e.g., -5 to +15
y <- y[event_time >= -5 & event_time <= 15]

# Add demographics
y <- merge(y, ind[, .(id, yob)], by = "id", all.x = TRUE)
y[, age := year - yob]

# Outcome construction
# Main outcome: log earnings; handle zeros by small offset or restrict to employed
y[, lnearn := ifelse(earnings > 0, log(earnings), NA_real_)]
# Optionally winsorize top 0.5%
q <- quantile(y$earnings, probs = 0.995, na.rm = TRUE)
y[earnings > q, earnings := q]
y[earnings > 0, lnearn := log(earnings)]

# Keep balanced pair-year observations (both parents observed same year) for primary spec
# This avoids differences in observation timing biasing within-couple comparisons
setkey(y, couple_id, year)
y[, n_in_couple_year := .N, by = .(couple_id, year)]
y_bal <- y[n_in_couple_year == 2]

# 4) Main regression: event-study DID within couples
# Specification: y_ict = sum_k beta_k * [Female_i x 1{tau=k}] + sum_k gamma_k * 1{tau=k}
#                + f(age)*sex + couple FE + year FE
# Omit event_time = -1 as reference category
main_fit <- feols(
  lnearn ~ i(event_time, female, ref = -1) + i(event_time) +
    poly(age, 3, raw = TRUE):i(female, ref = 0),
  data = y_bal,
  fixef = ~ couple_id + year,
  cluster = "couple_id"
)

# Extract and plot dynamic female-minus-male effects
es_coefs <- etable(main_fit, se = "cluster")

# Alternative: plot using coefplot
coefs <- coefplot(main_fit, keep = "event_time::female", plot = FALSE)
# Convert to data for ggplot (fixest >=0.11.2 has tidy-like methods; otherwise build manually)
b <- broom::tidy(main_fit)
b_es <- b[grepl("event_time::female::", b$term), ]
b_es$k <- as.integer(gsub("event_time::female::", "", b_es$term))
ggplot(b_es, aes(x = k, y = estimate)) +
  geom_point() + geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - 1.96*std.error,
                                   ymax = estimate + 1.96*std.error)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  xlab("Event time (years since first birth)") +
  ylab("Mother - father effect on log earnings (relative to t=-1)") +
  theme_minimal()

# 5) Long-run effect summary, e.g., 10 years after birth
lr10 <- tidy(main_fit)
lr10 <- lr10[lr10$term == "event_time::female::10", ]

# 6) Robustness check A: Difference-out father at the outcome level
# Construct couple-year difference outcome: mother minus father
# Pivot to wide then difference
wide <- dcast(y_bal, couple_id + year + event_time ~ female, value.var = c("lnearn", "employed"))
# female=1 is mothers, female=0 is fathers
wide[, d_lnearn := lnearn_1 - lnearn_0]
wide[, d_emp := employed_1 - employed_0]

rb_fit <- feols(
  d_lnearn ~ i(event_time, ref = -1),
  data = wide,
  fixef = ~ couple_id + year,
  cluster = "couple_id"
)

# Robustness check B: Exclude pregnancy years from reference and estimation
y_bal2 <- y_bal[!(event_time %in% c(-2, -1))]
rb_fit2 <- feols(
  lnearn ~ i(event_time, female, ref = -3) + i(event_time) +
    poly(age, 3, raw = TRUE):i(female, ref = 0),
  data = y_bal2,
  fixef = ~ couple_id + year,
  cluster = "couple_id"
)

# Optional robustness: Balanced 10-year window only
y_bal10 <- y[event_time >= -3 & event_time <= 10]
y_bal10 <- y_bal10[, .N, by = .(couple_id, id)][, .N, by = couple_id][N == 2]$couple_id |> 
  (\(ids) y[event_time >= -3 & event_time <= 10 & couple_id %in% ids])()
fit_bal10 <- feols(
  lnearn ~ i(event_time, female, ref = -1) + i(event_time) +
    poly(age, 3, raw = TRUE):i(female, ref = 0),
  data = y_bal10,
  fixef = ~ couple_id + year,
  cluster = "couple_id"
)

Notes:
- For employment or hours outcomes, replace lnearn with employed or hours.
- Consider also including first-birth cohort-by-gender fixed effects: fixef = ~ couple_id + year + interaction(female, first_birth_year).
- If you prefer to avoid any TWFE concerns, the “difference outcome” rb_fit is particularly transparent.

6. Expected Results
- Direction: The arrival of the first child will create a sizable and persistent increase in the within-couple gender gap. Mothers’ earnings and employment drop sharply around birth and recover only partially; fathers’ outcomes change little or may increase slightly.
- Magnitude (priors consistent with economic theory and prior evidence in Nordic settings):
  - Year 0–1: Large short-run drop for mothers’ earnings, on the order of 30–40% (leave plus reduced hours), relative to fathers.
  - Medium run (3–5 years): Partial recovery; remaining gap around 15–25% in log earnings within couples.
  - Long run (10+ years): Persistent gap of roughly 15–20% in log earnings; lower probability of promotion/managerial roles and slower occupation upgrading for mothers.
  - Fathers: Near-zero to modest positive effects on earnings/hours; small increases in hours or job stability.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (Event-study DID within couples)
- C1: Clear treatment timing (first birth) and correct assignment (mother vs father) — 1
- C2: Parallel pre-trends for mothers vs fathers within couples (assessed with leads) — 1
- C3: No coincident, non-child-related gender-specific shocks at event time (policy variation over time absorbed by year and cohort-by-gender FE) — 1
- C4: Stable sample/attrition not driving results (balanced panels, IPW, robustness to separations) — 1
- C5: Estimation addresses staggered timing concerns and dynamic effects appropriately (event-study with couple FE; robustness via outcome differencing) — 1

This plan delivers a transparent, testable, and policy-relevant estimate of the “child penalty” in Denmark as a widening of the within-couple gender gap in labor market outcomes following the arrival of children, with careful attention to dynamics and long-run persistence.
